stage: HISTORIE (engine stage 6) - fractal axis + competing frames - cache
disputedNote: Even where this story begins is disputed - picking a start date is itself a position. Frames change emphasis and annotation, never the record.

frames.label: Jun 2026 FAO-WFP report
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins on 16-17 June 2026, when FAO and WFP publish the new Hunger Hotspots outlook covering June to November 2026. The story reads as a present-tense appeal: 13 hotspots, a US$202 million ask, a US$695 million pledge from Washington, all measured against current funding gaps. UN agencies, wire desks like Reuters and AP, and outlets republishing them open here.

frames.label: 2023 conflict surge
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins with the conflict escalations that pushed Sudan, Gaza, Haiti and the Sahel into the 'highest concern' tier - Sudan's war from April 2023 and the Gaza war from October 2023 in particular. The story reads as a record of how active warfare, blockades and displacement turned chronic food insecurity into near-famine conditions. Al-Monitor, Arab News and humanitarian-desk reporters open with this frame.

frames.label: 2022 global food shock
frames.note: Under this frame the story begins with the 2022 grain and fertiliser shock after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, combined with the post-pandemic price surge and early El Nino signals. The story reads as a structural one: hotspots in 2026 are the downstream tail of a global food system already destabilised four years earlier. Down To Earth, development outlets and analysts tracking El Nino financing open here.

bands.label: Report and appeal
bands.summary: FAO and WFP release the June-November 2026 Hunger Hotspots outlook flagging 13 countries, with appeals for emergency funding and an early US pledge.

nodes.title: FAO and WFP release the June-November 2026 Hunger Hotspots outlook
nodes.what: The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme publish a joint early-warning report identifying 13 countries and territories where acute food insecurity is expected to worsen between June and November 2026. The agencies place Sudan, the Gaza Strip, South Sudan, Haiti, Mali, Burkina Faso, Yemen and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the highest concern tier, citing conflict, displacement, economic shocks and climate stress as overlapping drivers.

nodes.title: UN food agencies appeal for US$202 million to blunt El Nino effects
nodes.what: Alongside the hotspots outlook, FAO and WFP issue a US$202 million funding appeal aimed at shielding roughly 8.8 million people from drought, erratic rainfall and crop losses linked to the current El Nino cycle. The appeal targets anticipatory action in Southern Africa, the Horn of Africa and parts of Central America, where agencies say early cash transfers and seed support can reduce the depth of the coming lean season.

nodes.title: WFP welcomes a US$695 million pledge from the United States
nodes.what: The World Food Programme publicly welcomes a US$695 million contribution announced by Washington, framing it as a major boost to operations in the 13 hotspots as the report lands. Officials describe the funds as critical for food, nutrition and logistics work in Sudan, Gaza, Yemen and the Sahel, while noting the overall humanitarian funding gap remains wide.
nodes.disputed: Euronews and several wire desks describe the US$695 million as a fresh, timely pledge that helps cover the new appeal; some humanitarian commentators describe it as a partial reallocation of existing commitments rather than wholly new money, leaving the underlying shortfall largely unchanged.

nodes.title: Regional desks highlight Arab and Muslim-majority countries on the list
nodes.what: Arab News and Al-Monitor lead with the concentration of hotspots across the Arab world and wider Muslim-majority countries, noting Sudan, Yemen, the Gaza Strip, Somalia and parts of the Sahel among those flagged. The coverage emphasises how active conflict, blockades and currency collapses are translating into rising rates of acute malnutrition, particularly among children and displaced families.

nodes.title: Wire and regional outlets amplify the hotspots warning worldwide
nodes.what: In the day after publication, Reuters-sourced copy and independent desks from Down To Earth in India to Morning Star in the United Kingdom and AsiaOne in Singapore carry the FAO-WFP findings, reaching audiences across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas. The reporting consistently centres the figure of 13 hotspots, the El Nino appeal and the US pledge, while local outlets layer in national angles on food prices, displacement and aid access.

cites.l: Down To Earth via Google News

bands.label: Hotspot escalation
bands.summary: Sudan, Gaza, Haiti, South Sudan, Mali, Burkina Faso, Yemen and the DRC deepen into acute crisis as conflict, displacement and climate shocks compound.

nodes.title: FAO and WFP publish June-October 2024 Hunger Hotspots outlook
nodes.what: The two UN agencies release a joint early warning report flagging Sudan, the Palestinian territories, South Sudan, Haiti and Mali as hotspots of highest concern. The outlook ties the warning to active conflict in Sudan and Gaza, gang violence in Haiti and worsening climate shocks across the Sahel. It calls for scaled-up emergency food and agricultural assistance ahead of the lean season.

nodes.title: IPC Famine Review Committee confirms famine in Sudan's Zamzam camp
nodes.what: The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification Famine Review Committee determines that famine conditions are present in the Zamzam displacement camp in North Darfur, where hundreds of thousands of people are sheltering from Sudan's war. It is the first formal IPC famine determination in years and is attributed to fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces blocking humanitarian access.
nodes.disputed: UN agencies and the IPC describe the determination as a technical finding based on mortality and malnutrition data; Sudanese government officials at the time describe the methodology and the underlying data as contested.

nodes.title: Hunger Hotspots update covers November 2024 to May 2025
nodes.what: FAO and WFP issue an updated hotspots report extending the warning window into mid-2025. Sudan, the Palestinian territories, South Sudan, Haiti, Mali, Burkina Faso, Yemen and parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo remain on the highest-concern list. The report describes funding shortfalls as a binding constraint on the humanitarian response.

nodes.title: IPC warns of imminent famine risk across additional areas of Sudan
nodes.what: An IPC analysis published in December warns that famine conditions risk spreading from Zamzam to other parts of Darfur and the Kordofan region as conflict displaces millions and harvests collapse. Aid agencies report blocked convoys and looted warehouses. The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Sudan is described as the largest in the country's history.

nodes.title: FAO-WFP Hunger Hotspots report for May-October 2025
nodes.what: A new joint outlook keeps Sudan, the Palestinian territories, South Sudan, Haiti, Mali, Burkina Faso and Yemen in the highest-concern tier and adds further countries facing acute deterioration. The report links the worsening picture to a combination of armed conflict, economic shocks, weather extremes and declining donor contributions. It urges donors to front-load funding for the lean season.

nodes.title: Gaza IPC analysis describes famine conditions in parts of the territory
nodes.what: An IPC assessment for the Gaza Strip describes famine-level conditions in parts of the territory after months of restricted humanitarian access during the Israel-Hamas war. UN agencies appeal for sustained crossings and a ceasefire to enable food, water and medical deliveries at scale.
nodes.disputed: UN agencies and the IPC describe the finding as based on standard food security and nutrition thresholds; Israeli officials at the time describe the assessment as methodologically flawed and dispute the underlying access and mortality figures.

nodes.title: Aid agencies warn that 2026 funding gaps are deepening hotspots
nodes.what: Humanitarian agencies and NGOs report that contributions to Sudan, Yemen, Haiti and South Sudan response plans are running well below requirements early in the year. Cuts to bilateral aid budgets in several donor countries and the redirection of funds toward other crises are cited as factors. Country teams describe ration reductions and partial suspension of nutrition programmes.

bands.label: Global food shock era
bands.summary: The Ukraine war disrupts grain and fertiliser flows, prices spike, El Nino arrives, and acute hunger climbs across Africa, the Middle East and the Americas.

nodes.title: Russia launches full-scale invasion of Ukraine
nodes.what: Russian forces crossed into Ukraine from multiple directions, immediately disrupting Black Sea ports that handled a large share of global wheat, maize, sunflower oil and fertiliser exports. Shipping suspensions, port mining and a naval blockade halted grain movement out of Odesa and nearby terminals. Insurance and freight costs jumped within days, and fertiliser markets seized as Russia and Belarus signalled export restrictions.
nodes.disputed: Most governments and international outlets describe the action as a Russian invasion of a sovereign state; the Russian government describes it as a 'special military operation' framed around demilitarisation and protection of Russian-speakers.

nodes.title: FAO Food Price Index hits an all-time high
nodes.what: The FAO Food Price Index reached its highest level since the series began in 1990, with cereals, vegetable oils and meat sub-indices all spiking in the weeks after the invasion. FAO cited supply uncertainty from the Black Sea, soaring energy costs and fertiliser price rises feeding into 2022 planting decisions. Importing countries in North Africa, the Middle East and the Sahel saw bread and fuel costs climb sharply.

nodes.title: Black Sea Grain Initiative signed in Istanbul
nodes.what: Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia allowing safe passage of grain vessels from Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi through a monitored corridor. A parallel memorandum addressed Russian food and fertiliser exports. Shipments resumed in August 2022 and continued under periodic short renewals, easing some of the price pressure on global cereal markets.

nodes.title: Sudan war erupts in Khartoum
nodes.what: Fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, spreading from the capital to Darfur, Kordofan and Gezira. Markets, banks, bakeries and transport corridors collapsed in conflict zones, and humanitarian access narrowed sharply. Millions were displaced internally and into Chad, South Sudan, Egypt and Ethiopia within months.

nodes.title: WMO confirms El Nino conditions in the tropical Pacific
nodes.what: The World Meteorological Organization announced that El Nino conditions had developed for the first time in seven years. Forecasters warned of likely impacts on rainfall in the Horn of Africa, southern Africa, Central America and parts of South and Southeast Asia, with downstream effects on planting calendars and yields. Humanitarian agencies began revising 2023-2024 food security projections.

nodes.title: Russia exits the Black Sea Grain Initiative
nodes.what: Russia let the Black Sea Grain Initiative lapse, citing unmet conditions on its own food and fertiliser exports and on a Russian agricultural bank's reconnection to SWIFT. Strikes on Odesa-area port infrastructure and grain warehouses followed in subsequent weeks. Ukrainian exports shifted to riskier alternative routes via Romanian Danube ports and overland 'solidarity lanes' through the European Union.

nodes.title: Gaza war begins after Hamas-led attack on Israel
nodes.what: Hamas-led fighters attacked communities and a music festival in southern Israel, killing and abducting civilians and soldiers. Israel responded with extensive airstrikes and a ground operation in the Gaza Strip, sealing crossings and sharply restricting commercial imports of food, fuel and medical supplies. Within weeks UN agencies warned of acute food insecurity across the territory, with the north cut off from most aid.
nodes.disputed: Israeli officials describe the campaign as a military response targeting Hamas infrastructure and rescuing hostages; UN bodies, the International Court of Justice in interim measures, and Palestinian authorities describe it as a campaign causing widespread civilian harm and a risk of famine in Gaza.

bands.label: Hotspots monitoring framework
bands.summary: FAO and WFP build the joint Hunger Hotspots early warning process and IPC famine classifications become the shared language of crisis response.

nodes.title: Famine declared in parts of South Sudan
nodes.what: The UN, working with the South Sudan government, formally declared famine in parts of Unity State, the first formal famine declaration anywhere in the world since Somalia in 2011. The classification, made under the IPC scale, said about 100,000 people faced starvation and another one million were on the brink. Agencies described conflict and collapsing markets as the proximate drivers.

cites.l: UN News - South Sudan famine declaration

nodes.title: UN warns of four concurrent famine risks
nodes.what: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and humanitarian chief Stephen O'Brien warned that more than 20 million people across South Sudan, Somalia, Yemen and northeast Nigeria faced famine or famine-like conditions. The appeal framed it as the largest humanitarian crisis since 1945 and called for over US$4 billion in emergency funding.

nodes.title: SOFI report records rise in global hunger
nodes.what: The annual State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, jointly produced by FAO, WFP, IFAD, UNICEF and WHO, reported that the number of undernourished people had risen for a third consecutive year to about 821 million. The report linked the reversal to conflict, climate variability and economic slowdowns, signalling that progress against hunger had stalled.

nodes.title: FAO and WFP launch joint Hunger Hotspots process
nodes.what: Amid the first weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic, FAO and WFP began coordinating a shared early-warning framework that would become the Hunger Hotspots reports. The process combined IPC and CH food security classifications with conflict, climate and economic indicators to flag countries at risk of acute food insecurity deterioration over a forward-looking outlook period.

nodes.title: First formal Hunger Hotspots report published
nodes.what: FAO and WFP issued the first edition of the Hunger Hotspots outlook, covering March to July 2021. It named about 20 countries at risk of worsening acute hunger, with Yemen, South Sudan and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. The report established the recurring format - country tiering, drivers, and recommended anticipatory actions - that later editions would follow.

nodes.title: Famine conditions reported in Tigray
nodes.what: FAO, WFP and OCHA reported that more than 400,000 people in Ethiopia's Tigray region were experiencing famine conditions, with another 1.8 million on the brink, against the backdrop of the conflict that began in November 2020. Ethiopian authorities disputed the IPC analysis and rejected the famine characterisation, while UN agencies and aid groups described blocked access and a collapsing food supply.
nodes.disputed: UN agencies and aid groups described the situation as famine conditions driven by conflict and aid blockages; the Ethiopian government rejected the IPC findings and said food was reaching the region.

nodes.title: Hotspots report flags Afghanistan and Horn of Africa
nodes.what: The January 2022 FAO-WFP Hunger Hotspots edition added Afghanistan to the highest-concern tier following the August 2021 political transition and economic collapse, and warned of a fourth consecutive failed rainy season in the Horn of Africa. The report set out the conditions that would feed into the larger 2022 food crisis once the war in Ukraine began the following month.
